Research Question 2 asks which system framework and information security measures are appropriate for the cloud-based inventory and financial management system in terms of architecture, data security, user privileges, and data integrity and transmission security. The executed assessment found a working centralized framework with effective controls in the tested workflows. However, two reproducible authorization failures prevent an unconditional security-validation pass. The findings below identify what was observed, the controls that worked, and the conditions that must be addressed before a stronger suitability conclusion can be drawn.
Scope and Evidence of the Technical Assessment

The AI-assisted assessment reviewed the current repository and the connected KodiGo database on 27 October 2026. TypeScript compilation, ESLint, and the production build completed successfully. All 17 existing unit tests passed. A separate set of 22 controlled database scenarios produced 20 passes and 2 failures. Four anonymous browser-route checks and four HTTPS or API checks also passed. These results describe specific executed checks; they do not establish a population estimate, a questionnaire rating, or complete security coverage.

The database scenarios used synthetic Admin, Cashier, Inventory, Super Admin, and MFA-enrolled identities across two test stores. Every fixture write was enclosed in a subtransaction that was rolled back, and a post-check confirmed that no synthetic Auth identities remained. Role and JWT-claim simulation exercised PostgreSQL authorization and transaction behavior directly. Actual sign-in, real TOTP enrollment and verification, device integration, recovery procedures, sustained load, and concurrent-client stress were outside this assessment. The repository integration script was not executed because its dedicated service-role test credential was unavailable; the controlled SQL checks are reported separately.

Table 4.6 separates test families because they measure different properties. The 20 passing database scenarios and the 17 passing unit tests must not be treated as expert agreement or an acceptability score. Similarly, enabling Row Level Security indicates that a database control exists; it does not prove that every policy or privileged function is correct. Supabase documents RLS as the database layer for restricting row access and advises reviewing privileges and security-definer functions as part of the access model (Supabase, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

The examined framework uses a React and TypeScript browser application with Supabase services and PostgreSQL as the authoritative data store. Source inspection confirmed route guards and client state management, while live inspection confirmed database policies, business functions, and deployed user-management and invite functions. Centralized transaction handling addresses the fragmented records identified in RQ1 by writing related sales, stock, payment, and receipt information through server-side workflows. Bounded browser queues support selected interrupted operations, but a queued item is not equivalent to a committed database transaction.

The build and route checks show that the current application can compile and direct unauthenticated visitors away from protected pages. Large output chunks and mixed static and dynamic imports remained build warnings. These are maintenance and delivery concerns rather than observed authorization failures. The evidence supports the feasibility of the selected framework for the examined workflows, but no comparative evaluation of alternative architectures or scalability benchmark was conducted. Accordingly, the assessment does not establish that this is the most appropriate framework among all possible alternatives.

All 36 inspected public tables had Row Level Security enabled, and all eight public views used invoker security. In controlled tests, an Admin could read an assigned-store product but could not read the product in another test store. Anonymous product access was denied. The direct HTTPS product request and both privileged Edge Function requests also returned HTTP 401 without an authenticated session. Four local browser routes redirected anonymous visitors to the login page. These findings support the use of database authorization together with interface access checks.

MFA assurance was effective in the tested store-membership helper: an enrolled synthetic account at AAL1 did not receive store authorization, whereas the same identity at AAL2 did. However, the create_store_with_owner function accepted a store-creation request for that enrolled account at AAL1. This confirms inconsistent MFA enforcement across the tested privileged operations. The failed scenario should be corrected by applying the intended assurance requirement at the server authorization boundary of store creation and reviewing comparable functions. Supabase distinguishes factor enrollment from assurance-based access enforcement; both are needed for the intended MFA behavior (Supabase, n.d.-a).
Role Based Access and User Privilege Management

The controlled role tests supported the intended separation of everyday work. Cashier could read an assigned product but could not edit it or promote its own role. Inventory could update an assigned product but could not process a POS sale. An unassigned Super Admin could neither read a store product nor process a POS sale. A cross-store sale request was rejected, and an Admin could not delete the tested profile in another store. These outcomes demonstrate authorization in the tested database paths, without implying that every screen and operation received equivalent coverage.

A second failed scenario showed that the anonymous database role could call log_audit_event and insert a synthetic audit entry without an authenticated identity. This finding concerns the authenticity and controlled creation of audit evidence; it does not show that the caller could read or alter arbitrary business records. The function requires review of execution grants and caller validation. The Security Advisor also flagged 18 public security-definer functions executable by anonymous callers and 38 executable by signed-in callers. Those notices identify functions for review rather than 56 proven vulnerabilities, because an intentionally exposed function may still enforce appropriate checks internally.

The priorities in Table 4.7 are reviewer judgments based on the observed impact, not CVSS scores or participant ratings. The first failure bypasses the intended second-factor requirement for a privileged operation. The second weakens the trustworthiness of the audit trail and permits unauthenticated event creation. No production security configuration or application source was changed during this assessment, so the findings describe the pre-remediation state tested on the stated date.

The checkout scenarios provided direct evidence of transaction validation. A request with altered totals was rejected and left no sale row or stock change. A valid two-piece sale reduced synthetic stock from ten to eight and produced one receipt. Repeating the same sale identifier returned a single recorded sale without a second stock deduction. Requests with insufficient stock or an unassigned store were rejected. A later selling-price change did not alter the historical sale-item price. These findings support server-side validation, retry handling, and historical snapshots for the scenarios exercised.

The backend HTTPS connection negotiated TLS 1.3 with a certificate that passed verification at the time of the test. This demonstrates encrypted transmission for that inspected connection, not a complete audit of every supported cipher, hosting endpoint, or device. A targeted scan of 105 source, public, and generated client files detected no concrete private-key, Supabase secret-key, or service-role JWT format. That scan is limited to its defined patterns and inspected artifacts; it is not a guarantee that no credential exposure exists elsewhere.

The Security Advisor reported ten functions with a mutable search path and disabled leaked-password protection. It also identified the invoice_counters table as having RLS enabled without a policy. The latter does not by itself establish exposure: absence of an applicable policy normally denies direct row access, and a counter may intentionally be maintained through a protected function. These notices require review against the intended design. Relevant Supabase guidance treats advisor results as checks to investigate rather than automatic proof that every flagged configuration is exploitable (Supabase, n.d.-c).

Migration history and repository files were compared with live function definitions. The live MFA helper existed even though its migration version was not separately recorded in the inspected ledger. Conversely, the live refund function did not show the refunded_amount update present in the newer local refund migration. These observations show why deployment validation must inspect final definitions instead of assuming that either a baseline schema or a migration ledger fully represents runtime behavior. The refund difference was identified by definition inspection; its business effect was not tested in this exercise.

The assessment did not conduct a restore drill, penetration test, comprehensive storage-policy review, or real-account MFA challenge. It also did not establish an expert-survey suitability rating. Further verification should reproduce the failed scenarios after remediation, extend negative tests to other privileged functions, validate deployed migration definitions, and retain dated evidence for the corrected state. These conditions delimit the conclusions that the current evidence can support.

For the examined Kodigo implementation, a centralized browser and cloud-database framework with authenticated sessions, role and store restrictions, database RLS, invoker-security views, server-side transaction checks, and assurance-based MFA provides a technically supported foundation for the diagnosed SME workflows. The executed checks demonstrate specific working controls for access separation, stock consistency, historical records, and encrypted API communication. However, the observed MFA bypass in store creation and unauthenticated audit-event insertion mean that the tested implementation does not receive an unconditional security-validation pass. Its technical suitability is conditional on remediation and retesting, while comparative architectural suitability and the expert-rating component of the original RQ2 require separate evidence.
